# Agent Smith â€” Design Brief

## A native Windows connection-quality agent for gamers

---

## 1. Executive Summary & Product Vision

**Agent Smith** is a lightweight, native Windows desktop application written in Go that continuously monitors internet connection quality from a *gamer's* perspective and â€” critically â€” **localizes** where degradation originates. It does not sell a magic "lower your ping" button. It is an **investigator**: it hunts down what is degrading your connection and tells you, in plain language, *where the problem lives* and *what layer to fix it at*.

**The core concept.** Generic speed tests answer the wrong question ("how many Mbps?"). Gamers care about a different physics: small, frequent, time-critical UDP packets reaching the game server with low latency, low jitter, and near-zero loss â€” *even while the link is busy*. Agent Smith measures exactly those metrics, continuously, and runs a **bottleneck classifier** that attributes every lag event to one of five culprits:

> **Local machine** | **Wi-Fi** | **LAN/router** | **ISP access link** | **Upstream internet**

**Differentiation (from prior-art synthesis).** The credible tools in this space *measure and localize*; the dubious ones *claim to fix physics*. Agent Smith deliberately combines the strengths competitors leave fragmented:

- **Continuous** latency-under-load (Waveform/DSLReports measure it once; PingPlotter is continuous but not load-aware) â€” Agent Smith does both.
- **Per-hop localization** like PingPlotter, but with **ICMP-deprioritization awareness** so it never cries wolf over cosmetic mid-hop spikes.
- **Jitter and packet loss as first-class metrics**, not footnotes to average ping.
- **Per-process bandwidth attribution** (GlassWire-style) tied to latency events.
- **Local-vs-network disambiguation** (Wi-Fi RF + DPC/stutter awareness) so users don't blame the ISP for a driver hitch.
- **Honest remediation**: every verdict points to the *correct layer* (router SQM, Wi-Fi channel, NIC power setting, DNS) â€” never a black-box "optimize."

**Design tenets.** Lightweight, no login, no telemetry, runs unelevated by default, one-glance verdicts for casual users with depth for power users, and a hard refusal to ship the snake-oil patterns documented in Â§8.

## 2. Metrics That Matter for Gaming

Measure to the **actual game server** wherever possible â€” pinging a nearby speed-test node flatters the result. The four metrics below determine "feel"; throughput is merely a precondition.

### 2.1 Latency / RTT (dominant factor)

| RTT to game server | Grade | Experience |
|---|---|---|
| **< 20 ms** | Ideal (LAN-like) | Imperceptible; gold standard |
| **20â€“50 ms** | Great | Responsive; standard for competitive play |
| **50â€“100 ms** | Acceptable | Fine for casual; slight delay in fast FPS |
| **100â€“150 ms** | Poor | Noticeable lag; OK for turn-based/MMO |
| **> 150 ms** | Bad | Rubber-banding, broken hit registration |

**Genre overrides:** Competitive FPS (CS2/Valorant/Apex) target **< 30 ms** (pro **< 15 ms**); fighting games with rollback **< 30â€“40 ms** (â‰ˆ2 frames @ 60 fps); MOBA **< 50 ms** ideal / **< 80 ms** competitive; racing **< 50 ms**; casual/MMO/turn-based **< 100 ms** fine, playable to 150 ms+.

### 2.2 Jitter (often more disruptive than ping)

A steady 25 ms beats a 20 ms link swinging Â±15 ms â€” the game's interpolation buffer cannot predict erratic arrivals. Computed via **RFC 3550** smoothed mean-deviation (see Â§5.3).

| RTT jitter | Grade |
|---|---|
| **< 5 ms** | Excellent (competitive target) |
| **5â€“15 ms** | Acceptable |
| **15â€“30 ms** | Noticeable stutter / rubber-banding |
| **> 30 ms** | Bad â€” erratic, unreliable |

### 2.3 Packet Loss (UDP â€” a lost packet is a lost world-update)

| Packet loss | Grade |
|---|---|
| **0â€“0.5%** | Ideal (competitive target) |
| **~1%** | Noticeable â€” characters jitter, actions unresponsive |
| **~2%** | Frustrating â€” fast games hard to play |
| **â‰¥ 5%** | Effectively unplayable |

Bursty (consecutive) loss is worse than evenly distributed loss, and far more damaging combined with high jitter. Always count timeouts **separately** from latency samples.

### 2.4 Bufferbloat / Latency Under Load (the most commonly missed signal)

Idle ping of 15 ms can spike to hundreds of ms when *anything* saturates the link (a download, a patch, a housemate's upload). This is the classic "my ping is great until someone else uses the internet" problem â€” invisible to standard speed tests. Graded on **added (loaded) latency above idle**:

| Grade | Added latency under load (DSLReports Aâ€“F) |
|---|---|
| **A+** | < 5 ms |
| **A** | 5â€“20 ms |
| **B** | 20â€“50 ms |
| **C** | 50â€“100 ms |
| **D** | 100â€“300 ms |
| **F** | > 300 ms |

Measure **down** and **up** loaded latency separately (upload is often the worse offender). **Practical gaming target: A or B (â‰¤ 50 ms added).** C/D/F is a real bufferbloat problem. The fix is **not more bandwidth** â€” it is Smart Queue Management (SQM / fq_codel / CAKE) on the router.

### 2.5 Throughput Context (secondary â€” floor + headroom only)

Active game traffic is typically **well under 1 Mbps** (~40â€“150 MB/hour). Any modern connection carries the packets; ~3â€“6 Mbps down / 1â€“3 Mbps up is comfortable; 25â€“50 Mbps is ample headroom. Beyond the floor, **more Mbps does nothing for ping, jitter, loss, or bufferbloat.** Higher tiers only help *download large patches* and *share a household link*. Treat bandwidth as a precondition, never the headline metric (avoiding the "big download number" vanity trap).

## 3. Bottleneck Localization Model

The governing principle: **a degradation that first appears at hop N and persists through all subsequent hops is introduced at hop N.** A spike seen *only* at one intermediate hop, with later hops clean, is benign ICMP control-plane rate-limiting â€” **not** a real fault.

### 3.1 Layered probe targets

| Probe point | How to find it | Healthy RTT (wired) | If bad in isolation â†’ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Default gateway (LAN RTT)** | `GetBestRoute2(0.0.0.0)` / `ipconfig` gateway | **< 1â€“2 ms wired**, < 5â€“10 ms Wi-Fi; jitter < 1 ms | Problem is *inside your house*: NIC, cabling, switch, Wi-Fi link, or router itself |
| **First ISP hop (WAN edge)** | First public/CGNAT hop after gateway (traceroute hop 2) | **5â€“20 ms** (varies by access tech) | If gateway clean but this jumps and stays bad downstream â†’ **ISP access link** (congested node, bad coax/DSL) |
| **Public anchors** | `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1` | **< 30â€“50 ms** typical wired US | If gateway + first hop clean but anchors bad â†’ **upstream** (ISP peering/transit/backbone) |

### 3.2 Wired vs wireless detection

Determine the *actual* transport before assigning blame. `GetAdaptersAddresses` + `GetIfTable2` (or `Get-NetAdapter`) reveal media type, link speed, status; `WlanQueryInterface` confirms an active Wi-Fi link; `GetBestRoute2` identifies the egress interface actually carrying internet traffic. A wired link negotiating **100 Mbps instead of 1 Gbps** signals a cabling/port fault (damaged pair â†’ Fast Ethernet fallback) â€” a frequent hidden bottleneck.

### 3.3 Wi-Fi signal quality (when wireless is in the path)

| RSSI (dBm) | Quality | Gaming suitability |
|---|---|---|
| **âˆ’30 to âˆ’50** | Excellent | Max speeds |
| **âˆ’50 to âˆ’60** | Very good | **Ideal target for gaming** |
| **âˆ’67** | Working minimum | Lowest acceptable for stable real-time |
| **âˆ’70** | Fair | Gaming/streaming starts to suffer |
| **âˆ’80** | Weak | Unreliable; gaming generally won't work |
| **< âˆ’80** | Critical | Frequent drops; non-functional |

**SNR is often more decisive than RSSI:** > 25 dB sustains top PHY rates; > 20 dB acceptable; < 20 dB causes retries; < 10 dB poor/unstable. Strong RSSI with poor SNR (noisy environment) still produces retransmissions and lag. Watch the **PHY/link rate collapsing** (rate adaptation) and rising **retry counts**. Band guidance: 2.4 GHz worst (3 non-overlapping channels 1/6/11, microwave/BT/IoT interference); 5 GHz much better for gaming; 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E/7) cleanest. Wi-Fi is a shared half-duplex medium â€” contention forces MAC-layer retransmits, which surface as **jitter**: the #1 most common real culprit.

### 3.4 Local resource contention

- **Per-process bandwidth:** `GetExtendedTcpTable`/`GetExtendedUdpTable` (PID-owned connections) + gopsutil; catch Windows Update, OneDrive/Dropbox sync, Steam/Epic patching, torrents saturating the line.
- **CPU:** sustained **> 80â€“90%** starves the network stack and game thread.
- **RAM:** low available memory â†’ paging; watch hard faults/sec.
- **Disk:** active time near 100% / high response-time (ms) stalls disk-backed I/O.
- **DPC/ISR latency:** a misbehaving driver spikes local latency even when CPU/RF look fine (LatencyMon-style: max DPC < 2000 Âµs good, 2000â€“4000 Âµs doubtful, > 4000 Âµs unsuitable). Suspect when ping to the **gateway** is erratic but CPU and RSSI are healthy.

### 3.5 DNS resolution

Slow DNS *feels* like "the internet is slow" (pages hang before loading) even with fine ping/throughput.

| DNS resolution time | Rating |
|---|---|
| **< 30 ms** | Excellent (Cloudflare/Google median â‰ˆ 28 ms) |
| **< 50 ms** | Strong |
| **50â€“100 ms** | Acceptable |
| **> 100 ms** | Slow |

Test ISP resolver vs a public resolver (1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8); if public is much faster, the bottleneck is **ISP DNS**, not connectivity.

### 3.6 NIC health, MTU, offloads, power saving

- **Errors/discards:** `GetIfTable2` / `netstat -e` â€” healthy = at/near 0 and **not climbing**. Rising *errors* â†’ physical-layer fault (bad cable, duplex mismatch); rising *discards* â†’ buffer overruns/congestion.
- **MTU:** standard 1500; PPPoE/DSL often 1492. Mismatch â†’ fragmentation that specifically hurts time-critical traffic. Discover via DF-bit probing (`ping -f -l`, or `IP_FLAG_DF` in the ICMP API): largest payload that passes **+ 28** = path MTU.
- **Offloads/power:** for a latency-sensitive desktop, the throughput-favoring features that add jitter are commonly disabled â€” **LSOv2 (IPv4/IPv6)**, **Interrupt Moderation**, **Flow Control**, **Energy-Efficient Ethernet**, and the NIC's "allow the computer to turn off this device" power setting. (Checksum offload is safe to leave on.) Microsoft itself notes tuning interrupt moderation for throughput "may result in a performance hit on the response time." Agent Smith *detects and recommends* these â€” it does not silently change them.

## 4. Bottleneck Classification Decision Tree

**Inputs (per evaluation window):** `gw_rtt`, `isp_rtt`, `net_rtt` (RTT to gateway / first ISP hop / public anchor), `loss%`, `jitter`, `bloat_grade` (Aâ€“F), `wifi_rssi` (dBm, or N/A if wired), `cpu%`, `local_bw_sat` (link saturated by local processes? + offending PID), and `dpc_max_us`. Compare against EWMA baselines to detect *deltas*, not just absolutes.

Evaluate **top-down; first match wins.** This ordering localizes nearest-to-host first, because a near bottleneck masks everything beyond it.

```
# â”€â”€ 0. LOCAL MACHINE (host is the problem, not the network) â”€â”€
IF cpu% > 90 (sustained â‰¥ 3 windows)
   OR dpc_max_us > 4000
   OR (gw_rtt jitter high WHILE cpu%/RAM/disk saturated):
        â†’ LOCAL MACHINE
          (CPU/driver/disk starvation. If dpc_max_us>4000 â†’ name the .sys driver.)

# â”€â”€ 1. LOCAL BANDWIDTH CONTENTION (you are saturating your own link) â”€â”€
IF local_bw_sat == true AND bloat_grade in {C,D,F}:
        â†’ LOCAL MACHINE (self-inflicted bufferbloat)
          (A local process is filling the pipe. Name the PID. Fix: pause/limit it,
           then enable router SQM so it can't crowd out game packets.)

# â”€â”€ 2. WI-FI (only when wireless is the active egress) â”€â”€
IF egress == Wi-Fi AND (
        wifi_rssi < -70
     OR snr < 20
     OR (gw_rtt > 10 OR gw_jitter > 5) WHILE wired-equivalent baseline is clean
     OR phy_rate collapsed / retry_count climbing ):
        â†’ WI-FI
          (RF/contention. Fix: move closer, switch to 5/6 GHz, change channel,
           or go wired. Suspect this first for intermittent jitter on a laptop.)

# â”€â”€ 3. LAN / ROUTER (inside the house, wired path) â”€â”€
IF gw_rtt > 5  (wired)  OR  gw_jitter > 2  OR  gw_loss > 0.5%
   OR link_speed negotiated < expected (e.g. 100 Mbps on a gigabit port)
   OR nic_errors climbing:
        â†’ LAN / ROUTER
          (Cabling/switch/port/router-CPU fault. Check cable, port, router load.)

# â”€â”€ 4. ISP ACCESS LINK (your local loop to the ISP) â”€â”€
IF gw_rtt healthy
   AND ( isp_rtt jumps sharply above gw_rtt AND that loss/latency PERSISTS to net_rtt
         OR (bloat_grade in {C,D,F} AND local_bw_sat == false) ):
        â†’ ISP ACCESS LINK
          (Congested node / bad local loop, OR ISP-side bufferbloat under light local use.
           Bufferbloat with NO local saturation = the queue is upstream of you.)

# â”€â”€ 5. UPSTREAM INTERNET (peering / transit / backbone / server path) â”€â”€
IF gw_rtt healthy AND isp_rtt healthy
   AND ( net_rtt high/lossy OR jitter high at anchors/game server ):
        â†’ UPSTREAM INTERNET
          (ISP peering/transit or the path to the game server. Often outside your
           control; route optimizers MAY help only if the route is genuinely bad.)

# â”€â”€ DEFAULT â”€â”€
ELSE: â†’ HEALTHY (no dominant bottleneck; report current grades.)
```

**ICMP-deprioritization guard (applied throughout):** never classify on an intermediate-hop spike alone. A high `isp_rtt` only counts if the degradation **propagates to `net_rtt`**. An isolated mid-hop spike with a clean destination is router control-plane rate-limiting and is **suppressed** from classification (reported only as a diagnostic note).

**Confidence & multi-cause:** emit a primary culprit plus a confidence score; when two conditions fire close together (e.g. Wi-Fi marginal *and* upstream lossy), surface both ranked, rather than forcing a single answer.

## 5. Measurement Methodology on Windows

### 5.1 Probe protocol & the no-admin requirement

- **Raw sockets (`SOCK_RAW`/`IPPROTO_ICMP`) require Administrator** on modern Windows â€” avoid them.
- **Use the Windows ICMP Helper API in `iphlpapi.dll`** (`IcmpCreateFile` â†’ `IcmpSendEcho` / `IcmpSendEcho2` / `IcmpSendEcho2Ex` â†’ `IcmpCloseHandle`; `Icmp6*` for IPv6). The kernel builds the ICMP packet, so **no elevation is needed** â€” this is what `ping.exe` and .NET `Ping` use. Resolve the export dynamically via `LoadLibrary`/`GetProcAddress` for cross-version portability.
- Each reply is an `ICMP_ECHO_REPLY` with `RoundTripTime` (ms), `Status` (`IP_SUCCESS`, `IP_REQ_TIMED_OUT`, `IP_TTL_EXPIRED_TRANSIT`, â€¦), and `Address`. Allocate `ReplySize â‰¥ sizeof(ICMP_ECHO_REPLY) + RequestSize + 8`.
- **Primary signal = ICMP echo to the destination/game server.** Add a **TCP-connect probe to 443** when ICMP is filtered or when application reachability matters. Treat per-hop RTTs as diagnostic hints only.
- **Sub-ms resolution caveat:** `RoundTripTime` is quantized to whole ms. For fast LAN paths, time a synchronous `IcmpSendEcho` yourself with `QueryPerformanceCounter` while still using the API for the unprivileged send.
- *(Note: Go's `golang.org/x/net/icmp` unprivileged `udp4`/`udp6` datagram mode is Linux/macOS-only â€” **not implemented on Windows** â€” so the native ICMP API is mandatory here.)*

### 5.2 RTT statistics

- **Cadence:** fixed **~1 Hz** probe interval â€” frequent enough to catch transients, light enough to avoid congestion or tripping ICMP rate limits. Keep it jitter-free (required for RFC 3550 jitter). Count losses/timeouts **separately**; never fold a timeout into the latency distribution.
- **Aggregation:** rolling **5â€“10 min window** (300â€“600 samples at 1 Hz) â†’ `min/avg/max` + **p50/p95/p99**. Report **percentiles, not just mean** â€” the tail is what users feel. p99 needs hundreds+ of samples to be stable; do not compute p99 from ~50 samples.
- **EWMA** for the live needle and alert hysteresis: `ewma = ewma + Î±Â·(sample âˆ’ ewma)`, **Î± â‰ˆ 0.1â€“0.2**. Optionally run a parallel EWMA of deviation (mirrors TCP SRTT/RTTVAR, RFC 6298: Î±=1/8 SRTT, Î²=1/4 variance) for a smoothed variability band.

### 5.3 Jitter (RFC 3550 Â§6.4.1 / App. A.8)

```
D(i-1, i) = (R_i âˆ’ R_{i-1}) âˆ’ (S_i âˆ’ S_{i-1})
J(i)      = J(i-1) + ( |D(i-1, i)| âˆ’ J(i-1) ) / 16
```
where `S` = send timestamp, `R` = receive timestamp. The **1/16 gain** is a fixed-noise-reduction smoothing constant (â‰ˆ EWMA Î± = 1/16). For RTT-based jitter, substitute consecutive RTT samples: `J(i) = J(i-1) + (|RTT_i âˆ’ RTT_{i-1}| âˆ’ J(i-1))/16`. **Send at a fixed interval** (irregular cadence pollutes the estimate) and **exclude lost packets** from the recurrence (a gap is not jitter).

### 5.4 Bufferbloat load test

1. Measure **idle latency** baseline (anchor ping, ~10 s).
2. **Saturate** the link: sustained bulk download, then upload, then bidirectional â€” measuring loaded latency **separately for down / up / both**.
3. Report **added latency = loaded âˆ’ idle**, mapped to the Aâ€“F grade (Â§2.4).
4. Run on demand; additionally, **passively** flag bufferbloat whenever loaded-latency conditions are detected during normal use (e.g. anchor RTT climbs while a local process saturates the link â€” feeds `local_bw_sat` in Â§4).

### 5.5 Traceroute (TTL-limited ICMP echo, unprivileged)

Replicate Windows `tracert` (ICMP echo with increasing TTL, **not** Unix UDP) using the same ICMP API plus `IP_OPTION_INFORMATION.Ttl`:

1. For `ttl = 1, 2, 3, â€¦`: set `options.Ttl = ttl`, call `IcmpSendEcho2`, send ~3 probes/hop.
2. An exhausted-TTL router returns **ICMP Time Exceeded** â†’ `Status == IP_TTL_EXPIRED_TRANSIT`, `Address` = that hop. Record min/avg/max RTT.
3. Stop on `IP_SUCCESS` (destination reached) or a 30-hop cap.

**Caveat (drives the Â§4 guard):** per-hop RTTs come from router **control-plane** ICMP generation, which is rate-limited/low-priority. A high or missing middle-hop RTT is usually deprioritization, **not** a bottleneck. Only the **destination** RTT is a reliable end-to-end figure. Use `Icmp6CreateFile`/`Icmp6SendEcho2` for IPv6 (the `Ttl` field carries the Hop Limit).

## 6. Recommended Go Technology Stack

### 6.1 GUI â€” `lxn/walk` (primary), Fyne (fallback)

For a **Windows-only system-tray monitor**, **`lxn/walk`** is the best fit: genuine native Win32 widgets and a real **`NotifyIcon` system tray + balloon notifications** (the centerpiece of this app), tiny memory footprint, and a natural pairing with the direct `iphlpapi`/`wlanapi` syscalls. **Caveat: walk is stable but effectively dormant** â€” it still works on Windows 11 but expect no upstream fixes. If an actively maintained toolkit is preferred (accepting non-native widgets and a larger CGO binary), use **`fyne.io/fyne/v2` + `fyne.io/systray`**. If interactive live charts are the top priority and the WebView2 dependency is acceptable, **Wails** + a JS chart lib (uPlot/ECharts) has the best charting story.

**Charts with walk:** no native live-chart widget exists â€” render with **`gonum.org/v1/plot`** to an image each tick into a `walk.ImageView`, or draw a custom scrolling sparkline in a `walk.WidgetBase` paint handler.

### 6.2 Concrete stack

```go
// GUI + tray (native Win32, Windows-only)
github.com/lxn/walk          // native widgets + NotifyIcon system tray
github.com/lxn/win           // Win32 constants/structs (walk dependency)

// Windows syscall layer for all network APIs
golang.org/x/sys/windows     // GetAdaptersAddresses, GetIfTable2/GetIfEntry2,
                             // WlanQueryInterface, ICMP API, GetBestRoute2, PDH

// Telemetry / system stats
github.com/shirou/gopsutil/v4/net      // per-NIC IO counters (backed by IP Helper)
github.com/shirou/gopsutil/v4/cpu      // CPU
github.com/shirou/gopsutil/v4/mem      // memory
github.com/shirou/gopsutil/v4/process  // per-process

// Ping / latency
github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing  // ICMP echo + continuous prober (go-ping successor)

// Charts (render to image, show in walk.ImageView)
gonum.org/v1/plot
gonum.org/v1/plot/plotter
gonum.org/v1/plot/vg
```

Build with `-ldflags "-H windowsgui"` (no console window). For traceroute, prefer the **ICMP-API TTL approach** (unprivileged) over `github.com/aeden/traceroute` (raw sockets / needs admin).

### 6.3 Windows APIs to call (all unelevated unless noted)

| API (DLL) | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `IcmpCreateFile`/`IcmpSendEcho2`/`Icmp6*` (`iphlpapi.dll`) | Unprivileged ping & TTL traceroute |
| `GetIfTable2`/`GetIfEntry2` (`iphlpapi.dll`) | Per-NIC RX/TX bytes/packets, **errors, discards**, link speed, oper status |
| `GetAdaptersAddresses` (`iphlpapi.dll`) | Enumerate adapters: name, IPs, DNS servers, gateway, MTU, MAC, conn type |
| `GetBestRoute2` / `GetIpForwardTable2` (`iphlpapi.dll`) | Default gateway + actual egress interface for internet traffic |
| `WlanOpenHandle`/`WlanQueryInterface`/`WlanEnumInterfaces` (`wlanapi.dll`) | Wi-Fi RSSI, signal quality 0â€“100, Rx/Tx rate, channel, BSSID (query = no admin) |
| `GetExtendedTcpTable`/`GetExtendedUdpTable` (`iphlpapi.dll`) | Per-connection table **with owning PID** â†’ "which app is using the network" |
| PDH counters (`pdh.dll`) | `\Network Interface(*)\Bytes Total/sec`, `Output Queue Length` (Task-Manager-matching) |
| **ETW** (`Microsoft-Windows-TCPIP`/kernel-network), `GetPerTcpConnectionEStats` | True per-process bandwidth/retransmits â€” **requires admin/SeDebug** (opt-in feature only) |

**Rule of thumb:** read-only IP Helper, WLAN query, PDH, and the ICMP API all run **unelevated**. Only ETW per-process bandwidth and some kernel WMI classes force a UAC manifest â€” these are isolated to an explicitly opt-in advanced feature.

### 7.2 Roadmap

**MVP**
- Unprivileged ICMP engine (gateway + 8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1) at 1 Hz; EWMA + p50/p95/p99 + RFC3550 jitter + loss.
- Wired/Wi-Fi detection; Wi-Fi RSSI/SNR panel.
- Core **classifier** (Local / Wi-Fi / LAN / ISP / Upstream) with ICMP-deprioritization guard.
- Tray icon with one-glance color verdict + balloon alert on sustained degradation.
- Minimal dashboard: live RTT/jitter/loss charts + current verdict + plain-language remediation.

**v0.5**
- On-demand **bufferbloat load test** (down/up/bi) with Aâ€“F grade.
- **Traceroute** (TTL ICMP) + per-hop latency/loss view with deprioritization-aware coloring.
- NIC health (errors/discards/link-speed) and MTU discovery; DNS timing (ISP vs public).
- Per-process bandwidth attribution (PID-owned connections) â†’ catch the background hog.

**v1**
- **Lag-spike timeline / event correlation**: background logging maps a felt spike to *what happened* (which hop, which PID, an RSSI drop, a DPC spike).
- Passive bufferbloat detection during normal play; game-server auto-detection with genre-aware thresholds.
- DPC/ISR latency check (LatencyMon-style) for local-vs-network disambiguation.
- Historical scrollback dashboard; configurable alert thresholds; NIC offload/power-setting detection + recommendations.
- *(Opt-in, elevated)* ETW true per-process bandwidth.

## 8. Risks, Anti-Features & Privilege Considerations

### 8.1 Anti-features (the snake-oil checklist â€” hard "no")

- **No "lower your ping with one click" / magic-speedup claims.** Software can only reorder or reroute packets; it cannot make them travel faster than the route/physics allow. Anything implying otherwise is selling to "gamers who think RGB raises FPS."
- **No black-box "boost/optimize" buttons** with no measured effect (the Killer/placebo trap).
- **No local-only packet prioritization sold as a cure** â€” the bottleneck is almost always *upstream* of the NIC, exactly where reordering can't help.
- **No always-on service that hogs CPU, breaks apps, or silently re-enables itself** (the Killer Prioritization Engine lesson) â€” and **never** ship unsigned / HTTP-fetched config.
- **No vanity metrics** â€” download speed must never be the headline when latency/jitter/loss/bloat are what matter.
- **No forced login, telemetry bloat, or overlay overhead** dressed up as optimization.
- **No diagnosing a problem only to upsell a fix** â€” if we flag bufferbloat or a bad route, give the real fix path (router SQM, channel change, wired) rather than pushing a subscription tunnel that may not help.
- **No misleading traceroute panic** â€” never present ICMP-deprioritized mid-hop latency as a problem the user must "fix."

### 8.2 Privilege considerations

- **Runs unelevated by default.** The entire core â€” ICMP ping/traceroute, interface throughput, NIC errors/link-speed, Wi-Fi RSSI/SNR, gateway/route discovery, per-PID connection table, DNS timing, CPU/RAM/disk â€” uses no-admin APIs (Â§6.3). This is a deliberate adoption and safety advantage.
- **Elevation is isolated to one opt-in feature:** ETW/kernel per-process *bandwidth* (vs. the unprivileged per-process *connection table*). Ship a `.manifest` only if that feature is enabled; never demand UAC for the core experience.
- **Signing & supply chain:** sign the binary; never fetch config/definitions over plain HTTP; no auto-updating background priority lists.

### 8.3 Technical & product risks

- **ICMP rate-limiting / deprioritization** â†’ false positives. *Mitigation:* the Â§4 propagation guard + treating mid-hop RTTs as diagnostic only.
- **Measuring the wrong target** (speed-test node vs real game server) flatters results. *Mitigation:* auto-detect and prefer the live game server.
- **Percentile instability** from too few samples. *Mitigation:* enforce minimum sample counts before reporting p99; separate loss accounting.
- **walk maintenance staleness.** *Mitigation:* thin GUI abstraction so a Fyne swap is low-cost.
- **Sub-ms LAN quantization** in `RoundTripTime`. *Mitigation:* `QueryPerformanceCounter` timing on fast paths.
- **NIC offload/power changes are trade-offs, not universal wins.** *Mitigation:* Agent Smith **detects and recommends** with rationale â€” it never silently changes system settings.
- **Local-vs-network misattribution** (a DPC hitch felt as "lag"). *Mitigation:* explicit local-resource and DPC checks feeding the classifier's LOCAL branch first.
